title: Nobunaga's Gamble at Okehazama
text:
In the summer of 1560 Imagawa Yoshimoto, one of the most powerful lords of eastern Japan, marched west into Owari province with a large army, commonly estimated at around twenty-five thousand men. Owari belonged to Oda Nobunaga, a young lord of 26 whom many considered reckless. He had perhaps two or three thousand men to oppose the invasion, and his border forts were falling.

Nobunaga's retainer Ota Gyuichi, who wrote his life, describes the morning. Nobunaga refused advice to shut himself up in his castle. Before dawn he danced and sang lines from the play Atsumori about the brevity of life, armed himself, ate standing up, and rode out with only a handful of followers, collecting troops on the way.

Yoshimoto, pleased with his victories at the forts, had halted his headquarters near a hill called Okehazama to rest. His army was spread out over the countryside. Early in the afternoon a violent rainstorm swept the area. As it cleared, Nobunaga's men charged straight into Yoshimoto's headquarters. The Imagawa guards, caught off guard, scattered, and Yoshimoto himself was cut down and killed.

With its leader dead, the Imagawa army fell back and the house never recovered. Nobunaga's reputation was made. One of Yoshimoto's vassals, the young Matsudaira Motoyasu, later known as Tokugawa Ieyasu, broke away and soon became Nobunaga's ally.
lesson: A small force cannot win everywhere, but it can win at one decisive point. Strike where the opponent is complacent, and at the moment he least expects it.
people: Oda Nobunaga, Imagawa Yoshimoto, Tokugawa Ieyasu
source: Ota Gyuichi, Shincho Koki (Chronicle of Lord Nobunaga)
caveat: The size of both armies is uncertain, and historians debate whether Nobunaga attacked frontally or by the flanking surprise of popular tradition.
